title: Elton John backs Australian artists in fight against AI in surprise Aria awards appearance
text:
Elton John has made a surprise appearance at the 2026 Aria awards to draw attention to Not AI’s To Take, a major campaign backed by the creative and media industries calling on the Australian government to protect copyright law in the face of lobbying from AI companies.
Delivering a pre-recorded message at Australian music’s biggest night on Wednesday, the British singer backed the new campaign, which is calling on the Albanese government to ensure Australian artists are reimbursed and consulted by AI companies interested in using their works for AI training.
“I have long admired the talent and creativity of Australian artists,” John said. “So I want to send an important message to the Australian government. You have a duty to protect Australian artists and their work. Don’t let AI use any Australian artist’s work without full permission. Please, protect the next generation of Australian artists. Thank you.”
John hosted the very first Aria awards ceremony in 1987.
Australian musicians Jack River, Dobby, Josh Pyke and KLP also addressed the room at Sydney’s Hordern Pavilion on behalf of Not AI’s To Take, joining the likes of Jimmy Barnes, Paul Kelly and Peter Garrett who were among the artists who launched the campaign this week.
“It is not just lyrics and songs from Yothu Yindi, Missy Higgins, Gurrumul and Jimmy Barnes – you’ll be handing over Elton John, Beyoncé and the Beatles’ work too,” Dobby said. “Do not let Australia be the weak link that lets the world down.”
Not AI’s To Take is being supported by dozens of groups representing the recording, writing, publishing, film, television and media industries, including news outlets such as News Corp, Foxtel, Seven Media and Guardian Australia. The campaign warns that changes demanded by AI giants could put the $70bn creative industry and its 600,000 workers at risk.
“When Peter Garrett, The Guardian and Newscorp are all singing from the same song sheet, the Parliament should take notice,” said Greens senator Sarah Hanson Young in a statement.
The Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) is also backing the campaign, emblazoning the slogan on a billboard at the Hordern Pavilion on Wednesday.
“I can’t just go and film a movie at the movies. I can’t do whatever I want with other people’s IP,” musician Ben Lee told Guardian Australia on the Aria red carpet. “Corporations should be subject to the same laws. So if AI companies want to train on Australian music, it’s simple: pay us.”
Rapper Miss Kannina told Guardian Australia: “The Australian government doesn’t care about anybody but the billionaires, and they don’t care about artists especially. Any kind of opportunity the Australian government can get to make money, they fucking will.
“If you’re using datacentres and AI and shit like that, you’re not really an artist,” she added. “I think the Australian government would do a lot better putting a lot more money and time into communities and lower socioeconomic communities to do music programs and to really lift up the Australian music industry, because honestly, this thing is hanging by a fucking thread.”
Multiple music figures used their Aria speeches to address the threat of AI. Bluey composer Joff Bush, who won the award for best children’s album, paid tribute to the “real life human beings” who contributed to the show’s soundtrack, while Tim Minchin delivered a rousing speech in defence of “shitty, fucked-up, striving, stumbling, needy, petty, hopeful, heartfelt, fucking humanness”.
“Art is the way we reach out to one another, and it is defined and made beautiful by the glorious messiness of its human creators. This will only remain true if we assert it as true and act accordingly,” he said.
“Which is to say, AI can suck my balls,” he added to cheers.
Danny Rogers, the co-founder of Laneway festival, used his win for best music festival to call for urgent action.
“Original music and live music simply don’t exist without incredibly talented, dedicated and creative human beings,” Rogers said, adding: “The misuse of AI poses a real threat to our industry and things could change much faster than anyone realises. We simply cannot take human creativity for granted. We need to protect the people who make music we all love.”
While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has declared it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, and that artists “need to be compensated”, some AI companies have argued it is too difficult to make individual licensing deals under existing copyright law. AI companies have said they need legal certainty on the copyright issue before investing and training models in Australia, with Anthropic putting forward an “opt-out” model to scrape creative works unless a rightsholder objected.
A spokesperson for the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, told Guardian Ausrtralia on Tuesday that the government was “committed to supporting” creatives, and pledged any copyright changes would “deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”.
The government is expected to unveil a long-awaited legislative package on AI in late 2026 or early 2027, with proposals around datacentres, online safety, productivity and copyright.
